title: Rapid Handoff: SDK Lite Manifest and Checkpoints
content:
Purpose
---
This living note captures a super-minimal SDK onramp ("Lite") that the Solutions + DX teams can hand off to partners and internal integrators in under 30 minutes. The goal is to trade breadth for reproducibility: a checklist-driven, opinionated manifest with the smallest set of artifacts that let an engineer reach a working demo and collect useful telemetry.

Audience
- Internal SEs and SREs doing first-run customer integrations
- Partner engineers who need a low-friction sample integration
- New DX hires who need a repeatable first-week plan

High-level constraints
- Timebox: 30–90 minutes to a working demo (core happy path)
- Surface area: JavaScript + Python examples only (one serverless example + one container example)
- Observability: minimal telemetry baked in (latency, errors, token counts) that maps to Redwood Console metrics
- Security: show API key usage + recommend ephemeral keys for demos

What this package includes (manifest)
1) Quickstart README (single page)
   - 3 commands to run the demo locally
   - Expected output example
   - Troubleshooting triage table (network, auth, version mismatch)
2) Two sample apps
   - JS (Express + streaming example) — ./examples/js/stream-demo
   - Python (FastAPI + sync generation example) — ./examples/py/simple-gen
3) Tiny telemetry shim (1 file)
   - Emits minimal events to console and a local file: {route, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, latency_ms, status}
   - Hook mapping note: these fields map to Redwood Console fields: routeName, modelId, requestTokens, responseTokens, latencyMs, httpStatus
4) API contract snippet (one paragraph)
   - Input shape, output shape, error contract, retries suggested
5) Troubleshooting script (capture-env.sh)
   - Gathers env vars, quick curl health-check, node/python versions, pip/npm list trimmed
6) Rollout notes for SEs
   - Canary config suggestion, fallback model pair, and throttling knobs

Step-by-step quickstart (30-minute happy path)
- Pre-reqs: Node 18+, Python 3.10+, git, jq, small credit on a Redwood hosted account or local dev token
- Clone and boot:
  1) git clone <repo> && cd examples/js/stream-demo
  2) cp .env.example .env (insert REDWOOD_API_KEY)
  3) npm install && npm run start:dev
- Hit the endpoint:
  curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/generate -d '{"prompt":"summarize: product launch notes"}' -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
- Validate telemetry output (local file): ./telemetry/log.json (should show a single event with latency_ms < 500ms for local run)

Checklist for a successful handoff session (15–30 min walkthrough)
- [ ] Confirm customer has API key and region (note region in session notes)
- [ ] Run the JS demo and see streaming tokens in console within 60s
- [ ] Run the Python demo, verify the sync path returns JSON with text and token counts
- [ ] Attach the tiny telemetry log to the session notes and explain mapping to Redwood Console
- [ ] If error occurs: run capture-env.sh, attach to the ticket, escalate to eng-dx

Telemetry and evaluation suggestions
- Capture at minimum: request id, model id, prompt length, completion length, latency_ms, error code. Keep schema tiny so partners can forward logs without heavy processing.
- Add a small eval harness script (examples/eval/run_baseline.py) that:
  1) replays 20 prompts
  2) records token counts and BLEU-ish similarity to expected short outputs
  3) outputs a CSV ingestible by Optimize for baseline cost/latency curve

Open questions / known unknowns (to resolve before broad roll)
- What is the minimum telemetry retention we should recommend to customers for debug traces? (ops requirement vs. privacy)
- Do we provide a pre-generated ephemeral demo key service or point them to self-serve API keys only?
- Should Lite include a local model fallback (llama.cpp) for air-gapped demos? Pros/cons: makes demo offline-friendly but increases support surface.

Session scripts for SEs (scripted talking points)
- Minute 0–5: introductions + clarify intent (demo vs production test)
- Minute 5–10: confirm environment, copy .env, run example
- Minute 10–20: walk through telemetry output, show Redwood Console mapping and where to find token/latency breakdowns
- Minute 20–30: run one baseline eval, capture results, agree on next steps (pilot, Dedicated capacity, or full Private eval)

Failure modes and quick remedies (triage guide)
- Symptom: demo returns 401 -> likely API key or region mismatch. Remedy: verify REDWOOD_API_KEY & REDWOOD_REGION, check capture-env output
- Symptom: streaming stalls midway -> likely network proxy issue or CORS on browser demos. Remedy: run curl from terminal, try non-streaming sync endpoint
- Symptom: telem file empty -> shim not loaded; ensure instrumentation import line present in examples index.js / main.py

Follow-ups / next-iteration ideas
- Add a one-click cloud-run template (GCP) and an AWS Lambda + API Gateway quick deploy
- Add a single-page interactive playground that toggles batching, temperature, and shows cost estimate in real-time
- Build tiny terraform module for ephemeral demo infra with a short TTL

Session notes template (copyable)
- Customer: <name>
- SE: <name>
- Date: <YYYY-MM-DD>
- Region tried: <us-west1 | eu-west1 | ...>
- Model used: <meta-open-7b-v2 or similar>
- Telemetry artefact: link to uploaded log or attach to ticket
- Outcome: <demo-success | need-eng >

References and links
- GH PR with telemetry shim: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/213
- Jira canary ticket: ENG-1423
- Docs backlog page: DOCS-58
- Slack thread for handoff best-practices: https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C12345

Notes to self
- Keep the README under 250 words (people won’t read long docs during handoff)
- Default to safety: example prompts should be neutral and short (2–6 tokens ideal for quick latency checks)
- Schedule time with Maya to prototype the one-click cloud-run by 2024-05-10
